brief.summary: A personal record-keeper for adults teaching themselves the equivalent of a university degree from textbooks, open courses and lecture videos, which checks their logged work against a real degree's requirements.
brief.user: Marcus Bellweather, a 41-year-old warehouse shift supervisor who has spent two years working through an undergraduate mathematics curriculum on his own at night, using the published requirements of a state university's math BS as his guide.
brief.moment: He just finished the last chapter of a linear algebra textbook and wants to log the whole unit properly: the book, the chapters he did, the problem sets with his self-graded scores, the hours, and the two old exams he took under timed conditions. When he tried to mark the course complete, the record flagged that his hours look low for a 4-credit equivalent and that he never logged the prerequisite Calculus II exam. He needs to fix the missing entry, correct a problem set he logged twice, and decide whether this counts as complete or as complete with gaps.
brief.data: Target program: Mathematics BS, 120 credits, with 14 required courses and their prerequisites (e.g. MATH 220 Linear Algebra requires MATH 151 Calculus II). Marcus's record: 9 courses logged as complete, 2 in progress, each linked to resources (textbooks with ISBN and edition, MIT OpenCourseWare course numbers, YouTube lecture series), chapters covered, problem sets (e.g. Ch. 4 set: 32 problems attempted, 27 correct), timed exams (score, time limit, date, source), and total hours. Linear Algebra entry draft: textbook 'Linear Algebra Done Right', 3rd ed., chapters 1–8 and 10, 11 problem sets (Ch. 6 entered twice), 2 exams (78% and 84%), 96 hours logged against an expected 120–180 for 4 credits. Calculus II shows lectures and problem sets but no exam. A personal rule he set: 70% minimum on exams to count a course complete.

prompt:
I need the front end for Selfcourse. A personal record-keeper for adults teaching themselves the equivalent of a university degree from textbooks, open courses and lecture videos, which checks their logged work against a real degree's requirements.

Who's using it: Marcus Bellweather, a 41-year-old warehouse shift supervisor who has spent two years working through an undergraduate mathematics curriculum on his own at night, using the published requirements of a state university's math BS as his guide.

What they're doing right now: He just finished the last chapter of a linear algebra textbook and wants to log the whole unit properly: the book, the chapters he did, the problem sets with his self-graded scores, the hours, and the two old exams he took under timed conditions. When he tried to mark the course complete, the record flagged that his hours look low for a 4-credit equivalent and that he never logged the prerequisite Calculus II exam. He needs to fix the missing entry, correct a problem set he logged twice, and decide whether this counts as complete or as complete with gaps.

What's in the system at this point: Target program: Mathematics BS, 120 credits, with 14 required courses and their prerequisites (e.g. MATH 220 Linear Algebra requires MATH 151 Calculus II). Marcus's record: 9 courses logged as complete, 2 in progress, each linked to resources (textbooks with ISBN and edition, MIT OpenCourseWare course numbers, YouTube lecture series), chapters covered, problem sets (e.g. Ch. 4 set: 32 problems attempted, 27 correct), timed exams (score, time limit, date, source), and total hours. Linear Algebra entry draft: textbook 'Linear Algebra Done Right', 3rd ed., chapters 1–8 and 10, 11 problem sets (Ch. 6 entered twice), 2 exams (78% and 84%), 96 hours logged against an expected 120–180 for 4 credits. Calculus II shows lectures and problem sets but no exam. A personal rule he set: 70% minimum on exams to count a course complete.

Build it as a working web app, opened in the state that person would see at that moment. No backend: use realistic mock data (no lorem ipsum, no placeholder names), and make the interactive parts actually work client-side.

Use whatever framework and tooling you like. When you're done there must be a static production build in ./out with ./out/index.html as the entry point. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server (no rewrites, no server code) and viewed in a desktop browser at 1440×900.
